Abstract Recently, natural as well as synthetic polymers have been receiving significant attention as candidates to replace non-renewable materials. With the exponential developments in the world each day, the collateral damage to the environment is incessant. Increased demands for reducing pollution and energy consumption are the driving force behind the research related to surface-modified natural fibers (NFs), polymers, and various derivatives of them such as natural-fiber-reinforced polymer composites. Natural fibers have received special attention for industrial applications due to their favorable characteristics, such as low cost, abundance, light weight, and biodegradable nature. Even though NFs offer many potential applications, they still face some challenges in terms of durability, strength, and processing. Many of these have been addressed by various surface modification methodologies and compositing with polymers. Among different surface treatment strategies, low-temperature plasma (LTP) surface treatment has recently received special attention for tailoring surface properties of different materials, including NFs and synthetic polymers, without affecting any of the bulk properties of these materials. Hence, it is very important to get an overview of the latest developments in this field. The present article attempts to give an overview of different materials such as NFs, synthetic polymers, and composites. Special attention was placed on the low-temperature plasma-based surface engineering of these materials for diverse applications, which include but are not limited to environmental remediation, packaging, biomedical devices, and sensor development. Hemp fibers originated from Southeast Asia and further extended to China, where cultivation was reported to date to BCE 4500. Linen weaving and spinning were developed in Egypt in BCE 3400, and cotton spinning was started in India in BCE 3000. Sericulture (row silk production through the cultivation of silkworms) was invented and developed in China in BCE 2640, and later, silk manufacturing received attention all around the world. These historical facts are suggestive of the role of natural fibers in human life from prehistorical times. Fibrous materials, mainly cellulosic types like cotton, grains, wood, and straw, were often used in industrial applications and textiles. One of their most important uses was as a reinforcing material in polymer composites due to their abundance, biodegradability, cost-effectiveness, renewability, pliability, elasticity, less abrasive nature, etc. [2,3,4]. The role of NFs increased rapidly as time progressed, and now in the modern world, they have found applications in different sectors of life [5]. The uses of NFs were confined mostly to textiles but now extend to various interphases, composites, recycle strands, biodegradable matrices, micromechanics, biobased polymers, structural materials, and so on [6,7,8]. Like NFs, another class of important materials that play a significant role in applied engineering and technological advancements is synthetic polymer fibers. One of the major drawbacks associated with the usage of polymers is waste management [9,10]. fetched_contents.text: Importance of Interfacial Adhesion Condition on Characterization of Plant-Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Composites: A Review Abstract Plant fibers have become a highly sought-after material in the recent days as a result of raising environmental awareness and the realization of harmful effects imposed by synthetic fibers. Natural plant fibers have been widely used as fillers in fabricating plant-fibers-reinforced polymer composites. However, owing to the completely opposite nature of the plant fibers and polymer matrix, treatment is often required to enhance the compatibility between these two materials. Interfacial adhesion mechanisms are among the most influential yet seldom discussed factors that affect the physical, mechanical, and thermal properties of the plant-fibers-reinforced polymer composites. Therefore, this review paper expounds the importance of interfacial adhesion condition on the properties of plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites. The advantages and disadvantages of natural plant fibers are discussed. Four important interface mechanism, namely interdiffusion, electrostatic adhesion, chemical adhesion, and mechanical interlocking are highlighted. In addition, quantifying and analysis techniques of interfacial adhesion condition is demonstrated. Lastly, the importance of interfacial adhesion condition on the performances of the plant fiber polymer composites performances is discussed. It can be seen that the physical and thermal properties as well as flexural strength of the composites are highly dependent on the interfacial adhesion condition. Keywords: interfacial adhesion, plant fiber, methodology, characterization, polymer composites 1. Introduction Every year, hundreds of studies regarding plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites were published in various journals and the trend has been increased exponentially [1]. The application of plant fibers in polymer composites have drawn attention of many industry manufacturers [2]. Urgent call for ameliorating environmental impacts by reducing energy consumption and embedding biodegradability but retaining reasonable performances are the major driving forces for the development of plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites. In comparison with synthetic fibers, plant fibers offered multiple advantages such as light weight, biodegradability, low price, and life-cycle superiority. However, some drawbacks of plant fibers imposed challenges to the development and application of plant-fibers-reinforced polymer composites. With the collaboration between researchers, properties of the plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites is enhanced to a much greater extent. Matrixes are generally a homogeneous and monolithic material in which fiber and/or fillers system of a composite is embedded. It is completely continuous and provides a medium for binding and holding reinforcements together into a solid structure. The main purpose of matrixes is to offer protection and transfer loads to the reinforcement fillers [3]. On the other hand, plant fibers are held in place by the matrix resin, sustaining under high strength and enhancing performances of composites with almost zero cost. However, cooperation between plant fibers and matrix in a composite system relies on its interface conditions. Interface conditions are the prime factor of determining the properties of plant fiber polymer composites. This region experiences different thermal expansion during thermal processing and it acts as a barrier between the two distinct materials that differed in terms of physical and chemical properties. A composite with bad interface may find significant deterioration in mechanical and thermal properties. Even worse, inferior physical properties was also reported. Fortunately, numerous treatments or compatibilizers have been applied to the composites with the aim of enhancing physical, mechanical, and thermal characterizations. Alkaline treatment is the most widely used treatment on plant fiber composites because of its high cost-effectiveness [4,5,6]. It removes non-cellulosic components on the fiber surface and offering a clean but rough surface for better interfacial adhesion. Coupling agents and compatibilizers are deployed to promote more functional groups to enhance interfacial adhesion between fiber/matrix [7,8,9,10,11]. Through the abovementioned material modifications, researchers could improve conditions of interfacial bonding between the fiber/matrix’s interface, as illustrated in Figure 1. A good interface condition is facilitated by one or a mixture of four (4) interface linkage mechanisms, namely interdiffusion, electrostatic adhesion, chemical adhesion and mechanical interlocking. Interdiffusion bonding mechanism is governed by wettability. Optimum surface energy and polarity on both fibers and matrix, create permanent adhesion via Van der Waals, covalent, and electrostatic forces. Electrostatic adhesion uses attraction of cations and anions to form the interface. However, limited studies on electrostatic adhesion of plant fiber polymer composite were reported. Besides, improvement of hydrophobicity of the fibers via treatments may increase the chemical adhesion compatibility with hydrophobic matrix. Removal of fiber’s hydroxyl groups and substitutes with hydrophobic chemical bonding could assist to enhance the hydrophobicity of plant fibers. On the other hand, penetration of molten polymer into micron-diameter holes and adhered on irregular, rough fiber surface has created mechanical interlocking support system. This adhesive mechanism does not rely on any chemicals bonding or electrostatic forces, but the polymer acts like multiple hooks anchored on the fiber surface. fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of Silanization and Plasma Treatment in the Improvement of Selected Flax Fibers’ Properties Abstract The study investigated the effectiveness of the combination of chemical and physical methods of natural fibers’ modification. The long flax fibers were subjected to various types of modification. These were silanization, plasma modification and a combination of these methods. For the silanization process, two types of silanes were used: amino- and vinylsilane. The application of structurally different compounds allowed us to acquire knowledge about the effect of the modifier structure on its properties. Various properties of flax fibers were investigated, comparing the results before and after different modification processes. The flammability of prepared samples were tested by pyrolysis combustion flow calorimeter (PCFC). In the effect of the natural fibers’ modifications, flammability was reduced even by 30%. The thermal stability of modified fibers increased. The FTIR tests of the gases released during thermal degradation of the tested fibers allowed us to determine the important compounds and prove a lower degree of flax-fiber decomposition after modification. Flax fibers were also tested to evaluate their physical properties (linear mass, average diameter, aspect ratio and hygroscopicity). Changes in surface morphology were observed by scanning electron microscope (SEM). The properties of natural fibers improved significantly, thus contributing to an increase in their suitability for the use in composites. Keywords: natural fibers, modification, plasma treatment, silanization, flammability, thermal stability, scanning electron microscopy, fibers evaluation 1. Introduction Natural fibers are, among others, one of the fillers in the polymers, in order to improve the properties of the finished products. Polymer materials are an integral part of our everyday life. It is important to note that the usage of synthetic materials that are not biodegradable has polluted the environment to an alarming level [1]. Better awareness and willingness to care for the environment makes people more often turn to natural materials. Products manufactured from pure polymers are frequently replaced by those made from composites filled with natural raw materials. Decades ago, only the textile and packaging industries used natural fibers. However, advances made in the field of natural fibers and their hybrids constitue a worthy alternative to materials used in numerous conventional industries, such as the construction, aerospace or automotive industries [2]. Implementing natural-fiber-based materials instead of synthetic composites in a vehicle can result in a significant (up to 40%) reduction of weight. In this industry, many interior items were made exclusively of pure polymers, and this situation created a fire hazard. There can be many solutions to this problem, such as the addition of flame retardants or various types of synthetic, mineral or natural additives. Each approach has certain advantages, but the use of a natural filler in the form of lignocellulosic natural fibers seems to be the most appropriate one. Introduction In recent years, global awareness has prompted humanity to take action to preserve nature against various threats. These threats include air pollution, which contributes to global warming, water pollution, and the depletion of natural resources. As a result, many individuals are advocating for a different type of development and behavior through various laws that aim to increase the effectiveness of alternative fuels. This movement has led to the emergence of the concept of sustainable development [[1], [2], [3]]. Sustainable development is a widely recognized concept internationally, even though there is a lack of consensus on the means and methods of its development [4]. The concept emphasizes the need to consider both the current and future generations when making decisions. Eco-materials have been defined as a set of materials that should help reduce the environmental impact of human activities, and many researchers are working within this framework to develop eco-friendly materials that can play a leading role in promoting sustainable development [5,6]. The concept of eco-materials encompasses a wide range of materials, including both traditional and innovative options and their various uses. Developing and utilizing eco-materials is essential to achieving sustainable development and reducing the impact of human activities on the environment. Composites, due to their advantageous mechanical characteristics and light weight, are continually evolving towards products that are the most efficient and least expensive possible. They are widely used in various industries, such as the automobile, aeronautics, marine, and sporting goods sectors, among others [7,8]. To promote environmental protection and public health, composites are now being designed with an ecological character to reduce the use of materials made from fossil resources. The reduction of global warming gases also requires lighter materials and lower carbon emissions. As a result, there has been a shift towards using “environmentally friendly” and lighter materials, such as biocomposites, replacing conventional composite materials. Researchers focus on composite materials reinforced with natural fibers, as these composites combine good mechanical properties with low density [[9], [10], [11]]. These compounds offer several advantages, such as cost, availability of renewable natural resources, and biodegradability [12]. Moreover, many of these composites based on natural fibers exhibit mechanical properties suitable for technical fields [13]. The use of plant fibers as reinforcement of composite materials is increasing in various sectors of activity, like the automotive industry, where textiles have been used for years to reinforce the plastics used in cars, as they offer excellent insulation and are based on cellulose [14,15]. The use of natural plant fibers as reinforcement in polymer materials has limitations due to certain drawbacks, such as water absorption [16]. Plant fibers consist of lignocellulose, which contains hydroxyl groups, making them hydrophilic and unsuitable for use with hydrophobic thermoplastics such as polyolefins, resulting in poor moisture resistance. Furthermore, natural fibers can exhibit low dimensional stability, non-reproducible physical properties, and challenging processing methods that can lead to suboptimal final properties [[17], [18], [19]]. The main limitation of using natural fibers as reinforcement is the lack of compatibility between fibers and the matrix. Natural fibers' polar and hydrophilic properties are not compatible with the non-polar properties of most commercial polymers, such as unsaturated polyester [20]. When subjected to external stresses, composite materials undergo various types of degradation, leading to reduced mechanical properties. The degradation mechanisms are influenced by factors such as the tensile strength of the fibers, the matrix's energy absorption ability, the fiber-matrix interfacial properties, the volume fraction of fibers, and the applied mechanical stress conditions. Therefore, modifying the fibers' surface is crucial to improve their adherence to the matrix and reduce moisture absorption [21]. It has been demonstrated that appropriate physical or chemical treatments applied to the fibers can increase their compatibility with the polymer, enhancing the performance of the composites [22]. Several techniques, including alkaline, silane, and chemical treatments, have been utilized to increase the fibers' compatibility with the matrix. While composite materials reinforced with natural fibers are still in development and have limited applications, they are expected to play a crucial role in future industries, especially in construction [15]. The main objectives of this study are to provide an overview of natural fibers, their physical characteristics, chemical composition, and mechanical properties. It also explores the compatibility of natural fibers with different matrix, including thermoplastics, thermosets, ceramic resins, biodegradable polymers, bioplastics, and polymers derived from fossil resources. Furthermore, the performance and potential applications of natural fiber composites will be discussed in detail. Major fiber surface modification techniques used in natural fiber composites are best understood as a combination of chemical, mechanical, plasma-based, and sometimes sequential treatments, with silane coupling agents, plasma treatment, and alkali treatment being the most commonly used methods in the literature.

The most commonly used treatments are silane coupling agents, plasma treatment, and alkali treatment. Silane coupling agents are explicitly described as compatibilizers between fibers and matrix that improve bond by removing weak boundary layers and creating a cross-linked region [N1-R4]. Plasma treatment is presented as an environmentally sustainable procedure for enhancing surface characteristics of natural fibers, and the review emphasizes that it has received special attention for tailoring surface properties without affecting bulk properties [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Alkali treatment is also widely mentioned as a common and cost-effective treatment, often the most widely used in plant fiber composites, because it removes non-cellulosic components and offers a clean but rough surface for better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2].

By treatment type, the field spans chemical, mechanical, thermal, and plasma-based methods. Silane coupling agents are clearly chemical treatments [N1-R4][N1-R5]. Plasma treatment is clearly plasma-based [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Alkali treatment is a chemical treatment that is also sometimes associated with physical surface roughening [N2-F2]. The review evidence also notes that coupling agents and compatibilizers are deployed to promote more functional groups to enhance interfacial adhesion between fiber/matrix [N2-F2]. In addition, physical methods are described as clean, dry, and free from expensive and environmentally unfriendly chemicals [N3-F3]. The review of plasma research explicitly lists functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization as plasma processes [N1-F1], while the same source notes that low-temperature plasma surface treatment is used to tailor surface properties [N1-F1].

The functional groups or coatings introduced by these treatments vary by method. Silane coupling agents introduce silane-derived functional groups and a thin protective coating that can improve wettability and interfacial adhesion [N1-F3]. Plasma treatment can introduce hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy changes, and the review says plasma processing alters the natural fibers and sustainable polymeric derivatives for potential applications [N1-F1]. It also notes that plasma processes such as functionalization, grafting, and polymerization can alter surface chemistry [N1-F1]. Alkali treatment removes non-cellulosic components and exposes hydroxyl groups, while also creating a rough surface [N2-F2]. The review evidence also mentions that chemical treatments such as mercerization, acetylation, benzoylation, steric acid treatment, and silanization are used, and that silanization can introduce various chemical structures adapted to the polymer matrix [N3-F3].

Treatments are often combined or sequential. The most explicit example is the combination of chemical and physical methods of natural fibers’ modification, with silanization, plasma modification, and a combination of these methods being investigated [N3-F3]. The review of plasma research similarly suggests that multiple plasma processes can be used sequentially or in combination, including functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1]. The same source also says that plasma processing is used to alter natural fibers and sustainable polymeric derivatives for potential applications, which implies that plasma can be part of a broader surface-engineering workflow [N1-F1]. In addition, the interfacial adhesion literature notes that multiple interface linkage mechanisms operate together, including interdiffusion, electrostatic adhesion, chemical adhesion, and mechanical interlocking [N2-F2], which suggests that treatments are often selected to work synergistically with the fiber-matrix bond rather than in isolation.

In summary, the most common techniques are silane coupling agents (chemical), plasma treatment (plasma-based), and alkali treatment (chemical), with plasma also enabling grafting, polymerization, and other functionalization processes [N1-R2][N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-F3]. These treatments are often combined, especially chemical and physical methods together, and they introduce functional groups, coatings, or surface roughness that improve fiber-matrix interaction [N1-R4][N1-R5][N1-F3][N3-F3].

Surface treatments improve fiber-matrix compatibility by changing surface energy, wettability, and interfacial bonding. The evidence shows that interdiffusion bonding is governed by wettability, and optimum surface energy and polarity on both fibers and matrix create permanent adhesion via Van der Waals, covalent, and electrostatic forces [N2-R1]. The interfacial adhesion review also notes that chemical modification can increase surface properties such as wettability, adhesion, surface tension, and fiber porosity [N2-R2]. It further states that interfacial adhesion mechanisms include interdiffusion, electrostatic adhesion, chemical adhesion, and mechanical interlocking, and that a good interface condition is facilitated by one or a mixture of these mechanisms [N2-F2]. This indicates that the compatibility improvement is not only a direct surface effect, but also a multiscale interfacial phenomenon.

For plasma treatment, the evidence is especially strong on wettability and surface energy. Plasma treatment enhances the surface energy of fibers, improving wettability and adhesion properties [N3-R5]. The review of plasma research says that plasma processing alters the surface properties of natural fibers and sustainable polymeric derivatives, including hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy [N1-F1]. This makes plasma one of the most direct ways to improve fiber-matrix compatibility through surface wetting. The same source also says that plasma can be used for functionalization, grafting, and polymerization, which suggests that it can introduce chemical functionality that further supports bonding [N1-F1].

Silane coupling agents are also strongly tied to improved wettability and interfacial adhesion. The review states that silanization can improve water resistance, increase surface wettability of natural fibers by polymers, and promote interfacial adhesion [N3-F3]. The same source notes that silane treatment is often used to improve the properties of natural fibers, including flammability, thermal stability, and wettability [N3-F3]. It also says that silane coupling agents are used as compatibilizers between fibers and matrix [N1-R4]. This means silane is not only a chemical treatment, but also a method of introducing specific functional groups that can bridge the fiber and matrix.

Alkali treatment improves compatibility through roughening and cleaning. The interfacial adhesion review describes alkali treatment as the most widely used treatment because it removes non-cellulosic components and offers a clean but rough surface for better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2]. This roughness increases the area available for mechanical interlocking and improves contact between fiber and matrix, which is part of why alkali-treated fibers are often used [N2-F2]. The review also says that chemical treatments such as mercerization, acetylation, benzoylation, steric acid treatment, and silanization are used to increase compatibility with matrix [N3-F3], and that silanization has a positive effect on interfacial adhesion [N3-F3]. This shows that alkali treatment can be complementary to other treatments rather than a standalone solution.

Evidence for improved interfacial bonding and mechanical performance comes from multiple sources. The interfacial adhesion review states that appropriate physical or chemical treatments applied to the fibers can increase their compatibility with the polymer, enhancing the performance of the composites [N2-F2]. It also notes that fiber-matrix interfacial adhesion is among the most influential factors affecting the physical, mechanical, and thermal properties of plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites [N2-F2]. In the plasma study, the review says that plasma treatment improves the wettability and adhesion properties of fibers, which is particularly relevant for compatibility with matrix systems [N3-R5]. The silanization study reports that modified fibers show improved properties such as flammability reduction, thermal stability, and wettability, contributing to their suitability for composites [N3-F3]. The review of natural fibers and composites similarly says that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the matrix and enhance composite performance [N4-F4]. This pattern across sources supports the conclusion that treatments are effective when they improve both surface wettability and the underlying interfacial bond.

Known limitations or trade-offs are also evident. Plasma treatment is described as an environmentally sustainable procedure, but the evidence also notes that initial system costs can be high and operators may face operational constraints [N3-F3]. Alkali treatment is noted as highly cost-effective [N2-F2], but it is also a chemical treatment that can leave residual chemicals or require careful post-treatment handling. Silane coupling agents are effective but may be less scalable or more expensive than some physical methods [N1-R4][N3-F3]. The review of plasma research also notes that plasma processes are being used to replace environmentally hazardous chemicals, but this implies that the environmental benefit is part of the trade-off [N1-F1]. In general, the literature suggests that effectiveness often comes with a balance of cost, scalability, and environmental impact, rather than a single ideal solution [N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence shows that surface treatments improve compatibility by increasing surface energy and wettability, introducing functional groups or coatings that promote adhesion, and enabling mechanical interlocking and interdiffusion bonding [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N3-R5][N3-F3]. They also improve mechanical performance and reduce limitations such as poor adhesion, moisture absorption, and flammability, but they do so with trade-offs in cost, scalability, and environmental impact [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

Treated natural fibers are used in a wide range of industries and composite systems, including construction, automotive, aerospace, marine, and packaging. The review of natural fibers and composites states that natural fiber composites are eco-friendly alternatives to conventional materials and are used in the automobile, aeronautics, marine, and sporting goods sectors [N4-F4]. It also notes that they are expected to play a crucial role in construction [N4-F4]. The review of natural fibers and their composites adds that these composites combine good mechanical properties with low density and are used in various industries, including the automobile, aeronautics, marine, and sporting goods sectors [N4-F4]. The same review emphasizes that natural fibers are used in composites reinforced with thermoplastics, thermosets, ceramic resins, biodegradable polymers, bioplastics, and polymers derived from fossil resources [N4-F4]. This indicates that treated natural fibers are not limited to a single matrix system but are integrated across a broad family of polymer matrices.

A specific example from the evidence is banana and sisal fiber-reinforced epoxy biocomposites, which were studied for structural applications [N4-F4]. The review also discusses hemp and banana fiber-fabric-reinforced polymer composites suitable for exterior-engineered parts [N4-R2]. These examples show that treated natural fibers are used in structural and exterior applications, not only as textiles but also in load-bearing or durable composite systems. The review further notes that natural fibers are used in interior insulation, seat bottom, door panels, dashboard, body panels, boot liner, and other automotive components [N3-F3], which underscores the automotive industry’s reliance on treated natural fibers for lightweight, biodegradable, and flammability-reduced parts.

Cost and scalability considerations are a major theme. Alkali treatment is described as highly cost-effective [N2-F2], which makes it attractive for industrial adoption. However, the same source notes that chemical treatments can be expensive and may require careful handling [N2-F2]. The plasma study says that physical methods are clean, dry, and free from expensive and environmentally unfriendly chemicals, but it also notes that initial system costs can be high and operators may face operational constraints [N3-F3]. This trade-off is important because scalability depends on whether the treatment can be applied efficiently at scale. The review of natural fibers and composites further says that the main limitation of natural fibers as reinforcement is the lack of compatibility between fibers and matrix, and that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility and enhance composite performance [N4-F4]. This implies that industrial adoption is constrained by both the need for effective treatment and the feasibility of applying it economically and at scale.

Environmental and sustainability implications are strong. The review says that natural fibers are eco-friendly, renewable, and biodegradable, and that natural fiber composites are promoted as sustainable materials that reduce environmental impact and support sustainable development [N4-F4]. The same review states that natural fibers reduce the carbon footprint of building materials and enhance the overall sustainability of construction [N6-R2]. Plasma treatment is presented as an environmentally sustainable procedure and as a way to reduce environmentally hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. The review of natural fibers and composites also notes that the use of natural fibers can reduce global warming gases, lower carbon emissions, and support the shift toward lighter, less carbon-intensive materials [N4-F4]. In contrast, the evidence for alkali and silane treatments is more mixed: while alkali treatment is cost-effective, it is also a chemical treatment that may have environmental drawbacks relative to plasma-based alternatives [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The broader environmental assessment also notes that fiber-reinforced composites face significant environmental challenges throughout their lifecycle, from raw material extraction to end-of-life [N6-R4]. This means that treated natural fibers are not only about improving mechanical properties; they are also part of a broader sustainability strategy.

In practical terms, the evidence supports a picture of treated natural fibers being deployed in construction, automotive, aerospace, marine, and packaging industries, with composites including thermoplastics, thermosets, biodegradable polymers, and epoxy systems [N4-F4]. The main cost and scalability issues are that some treatments are expensive or operationally demanding, while others are cleaner but may require high initial investment [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The environmental implication is that treated natural fibers are part of a sustainable materials strategy, but adoption depends on balancing mechanical performance, cost, and lifecycle environmental impact [N4-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Recent trends and emerging approaches in fiber surface modification are moving toward bio-inspired coatings, nanoscale functionalization, and more sustainable and scalable methods. The most directly relevant emerging approach is bio-inspired coatings for natural fiber composites, which the review explicitly says examines recent advancements in bio-inspired coatings and their unique properties [N5-R1]. The review also notes that plasma surface engineering is a long-standing but still evolving area, with recent developments including functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1]. These indicate that the field is expanding beyond traditional silane and plasma treatments into more specialized and tailored surface engineering.

A major novelty of these emerging approaches is the ability to create coatings and functional groups that are specifically adapted to the fiber-matrix interface. The bio-inspired coatings review emphasizes a range of innovative coatings, suggesting that the focus is not just on surface roughness or cleaning, but on designing coatings that match the functional needs of the composite system [N5-R1]. The surface modification review of bio-based composites via silane treatment also points to recent insights into mechanical and thermal properties, showing that silane is still central but increasingly understood in terms of its interfacial and functional role [N5-R4]. The review of surface and interfacial engineering of biosourced fillers likewise highlights recent developments in nanocellulose and 2D materials such as graphene, indicating that the field is moving toward nanoscale and hybrid interfacial engineering [N5-R3]. These trends suggest that the next generation of modification is not just about improving wettability, but about creating smart, bio-inspired, and nano-functionalized surfaces.

These emerging approaches address existing limitations in several ways. One limitation of traditional treatments is that they can be expensive, environmentally demanding, or limited in scalability. Plasma treatment is described as environmentally sustainable and as a way to replace environmentally hazardous chemicals [N1-F1], while the evidence for alkali and silane treatments highlights cost-effectiveness and scalability concerns [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Emerging approaches can mitigate these issues by using cleaner processes or by combining treatments in ways that reduce reliance on costly or toxic chemicals. The evidence also shows that treatments can be combined or sequential, such as chemical and physical methods together, which can optimize performance while reducing the burden of a single treatment [N3-F3]. The plasma review further notes that low-temperature plasma can tailor surface properties without affecting bulk properties, which is important for preserving the integrity of the fiber and matrix while improving interface quality [N1-F1]. This addresses the limitation that some treatments may alter the bulk material in unintended ways.

Another limitation is poor interfacial adhesion, moisture absorption, and flammability. The review of natural fibers and composites says that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the matrix and enhance composite performance [N4-F4], and that natural fibers can exhibit poor moisture resistance and low dimensional stability [N4-F4]. The plasma study says that plasma treatment improves wettability and adhesion properties, which is particularly relevant for compatibility with hydrophobic matrices [N3-R5]. Silanization is reported to improve water resistance, increase surface wettability, promote interfacial adhesion, and reduce flammability [N3-F3]. Emerging approaches such as bio-inspired coatings and nanoscale functionalization are positioned to address these limitations by introducing more precise control over surface chemistry and interfacial bonding [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The evidence also suggests that these methods are increasingly being evaluated for a broader range of applications, including environmental remediation, packaging, biomedical devices, and sensor development [N1-F1]. This indicates that the field is broadening beyond traditional composites into more functional and sustainable materials.

In terms of commercial or industrial adoption, plasma treatment appears closest to commercial use because it is already described as an environmentally sustainable procedure and is being used to replace hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. Silane coupling agents are also well established and widely used, as they are explicitly described as common compatibilizers [N1-R4][N1-R5]. Alkali treatment is highly cost-effective and therefore attractive for industrial adoption, although it may still be limited by chemical residues or process constraints [N2-F2]. The emerging approaches such as bio-inspired coatings and nanoscale functionalization are still more research-oriented than fully industrialized, but the evidence suggests they are increasingly being evaluated for practical applications [N5-R1][N5-R3]. ## Integrated summary of fiber surface modification techniques for natural fiber/polymer compatibility

Natural fiber composites are attractive because natural fibers are renewable, lightweight, and biodegradable, but they often have poor compatibility with polymer matrices due to differences in polarity, hydrophilicity, and surface chemistry. The literature shows that surface modification is the primary way to bridge this gap. The best-supported conclusion is that the major fiber surface modification techniques are **chemical, plasma-based, and mechanical/physical methods**, with **silane coupling agents**, **plasma treatment**, and **alkali treatment** being the most commonly used and most explicitly discussed in the evidence [N1-R4][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 1) Common modification techniques and their classification

The evidence identifies a clear inventory of major techniques:

- **Silane coupling agents**: These are explicitly described as compatibilizers between fibers and matrix that improve bond by removing weak boundary layers and creating a cross-linked region [N1-R4]. They are also among the most common chemical treatments, and silanization is noted as a widely used method to improve wettability and interfacial adhesion [N1-R5][N3-F3]. Silane treatment introduces **silane-derived functional groups** and a **thin protective coating**, which can improve wettability and interfacial bonding [N1-F3].

- **Plasma treatment**: This is described as an environmentally sustainable procedure for enhancing the surface characteristics of natural fibers [N1-R2]. The review explicitly states that low-temperature plasma surface treatment is used to tailor surface properties without affecting bulk properties [N1-F1]. Plasma processes include functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1]. Plasma treatment is especially associated with improving **hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy** [N1-F1][N3-R5].

- **Alkali treatment**: This is presented as a widely used and highly cost-effective treatment that removes non-cellulosic components and provides a clean but rough surface for better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2]. It is also part of the broader set of chemical treatments used to improve compatibility [N3-F3].

- **Other chemical and physical methods**: The evidence also mentions **mercierization, acetylation, benzoylation, steric acid treatment, and silanization** as chemical treatments, while physical methods are described as clean, dry, and free from expensive and environmentally unfriendly chemicals [N3-F3]. The interfacial adhesion review also notes that chemical modification can increase surface properties such as wettability, adhesion, surface tension, and fiber porosity [N2-R2].

- **Sequential or combined treatments**: The evidence repeatedly shows that treatments are often used **together** rather than in isolation. A clear example is the combination of **chemical and physical methods**, with silanization, plasma modification, and a combination of these methods being investigated [N3-F3]. Plasma research similarly suggests that multiple plasma processes can be used sequentially or in combination, including functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1].

### 2) How these techniques improve fiber-matrix compatibility

Surface treatments improve compatibility by altering **surface energy, wettability, and interfacial bonding**, and the evidence supports this with several overlapping mechanisms.

- **Wettability and surface energy**: Interdiffusion bonding is governed by wettability, and optimum surface energy and polarity on both fibers and matrix create permanent adhesion via Van der Waals, covalent, and electrostatic forces [N2-R1]. Chemical modification can also increase wettability, adhesion, surface tension, and fiber porosity [N2-R2]. Plasma treatment improves the surface energy of fibers, thereby improving their wettability and adhesion properties [N3-R5]. Plasma processing also alters natural fibers and sustainable polymeric derivatives for potential applications by changing hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy [N1-F1].

- **Interfacial bonding and mechanical performance**: The interfacial adhesion review states that appropriate physical or chemical treatments applied to the fibers can increase their compatibility with the polymer and enhance composite performance [N2-F2]. It also notes that fiber-matrix interfacial adhesion is among the most influential factors affecting the physical, mechanical, and thermal properties of plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites [N2-F2]. Silanization is reported to improve water resistance, increase surface wettability of natural fibers by polymers, and promote interfacial adhesion [N3-F3]. The review of natural fibers and composites similarly says that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the matrix and enhance composite performance [N4-F4].

- **Mechanical interlocking and roughness**: Alkali treatment creates a clean but rough surface, which increases the area available for mechanical interlocking and improves contact between fiber and matrix [N2-F2]. This roughness is part of why alkali-treated fibers are often used [N2-F2].

### 3) Evidence for improved interfacial bonding and mechanical performance

The evidence across the branch reports is consistent that treatments improve mechanical performance. For example:

- The plasma study reports that plasma treatment improves the wettability and adhesion properties of fibers, which is particularly relevant for compatibility with matrix systems [N3-R5].
- Silanization is reported to improve flammability, thermal stability, and wettability, contributing to the suitability of modified fibers for composites [N3-F3].
- The interfacial adhesion review explicitly states that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the polymer and enhance composite performance [N2-F2].
- The natural fiber composites review says that natural fiber composites combine good mechanical properties with low density and are used in various industries [N4-F4].

### 4) Known limitations and trade-offs

The evidence also makes clear that no single treatment is perfect. Each method has trade-offs:

- **Cost and scalability**: Alkali treatment is highly cost-effective [N2-F2], but other chemical treatments can be expensive and may require careful handling [N2-F2]. Physical methods are clean and dry but can have high initial system costs and operational constraints [N3-F3].
- **Environmental impact**: Plasma treatment is presented as environmentally sustainable and as a way to replace environmentally hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. However, the broader lifecycle of fiber-reinforced composites is still environmentally significant, with challenges from raw material extraction to end-of-life [N6-R4]. Natural fibers are eco-friendly and renewable, but they can still be limited by poor compatibility, moisture absorption, and flammability [N4-F4].
- **Functional specificity**: Silane coupling agents are effective and widely used, but they may be less scalable or more expensive than some physical methods [N1-R4][N3-F3]. Plasma treatment is effective and environmentally attractive, but its adoption depends on equipment costs and process constraints [N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests that the most effective strategy is often to combine chemical and physical treatments rather than rely on a single method [N3-F3].

### 5) Practical relevance and real-world application context

Treated natural fibers are already being used in a wide range of industries and composite systems:

- **Construction**: Natural fibers are described as reducing the carbon footprint of building materials and enhancing sustainability in construction [N6-R2].
- **Automotive**: Treated fibers are used in interior insulation, seat bottom, door panels, dashboard, body panels, boot liner, and other automotive components [N3-F3].
- **Aerospace, marine, and sporting goods**: The review says natural fiber composites are used in these sectors and are promoted as eco-friendly alternatives to conventional materials [N4-F4].
- **Packaging and structural applications**: Banana and sisal fiber-reinforced epoxy biocomposites were studied for structural applications [N4-F4], and hemp and banana fiber-fabric-reinforced polymer composites were studied for exterior-engineered parts [N4-R2].

The evidence also shows that treated natural fibers are used with a broad range of polymer matrices, including thermoplastics, thermosets, biodegradable polymers, bioplastics, and polymers derived from fossil resources [N4-F4]. This indicates that the compatibility improvements are not limited to a single matrix system.

### 6) Recent trends and emerging approaches

The evidence points to several recent trends that go beyond the traditional silane and plasma approaches:

- **Bio-inspired coatings**: One emerging approach is bio-inspired coatings for natural fiber composites, which the review says examines recent advancements in bio-inspired coatings and their unique properties [N5-R1].
- **Nanoscale functionalization**: The review of surface and interfacial engineering of biosourced fillers highlights recent developments in nanocellulose and 2D materials like graphene [N5-R3]. This suggests a shift toward more precise, nanoscale control of the fiber-matrix interface.
- **Silane-based surface modification**: Silane treatment is still central, but the evidence shows that it is increasingly understood in terms of mechanical, thermal, and interfacial properties [N5-R4].
- **Plasma surface engineering**: Plasma remains a major trend because it can functionalize, graft, polymerize, and otherwise alter surface chemistry in a controlled way [N1-F1].

These emerging approaches address existing limitations in several ways:

- They can improve precision and specificity of the surface chemistry introduced.
- They can reduce reliance on costly or toxic chemicals.
- They can address poor adhesion, moisture absorption, and flammability.
- They can support broader sustainability goals by using cleaner processes and bio-inspired designs.

### 7) Which approaches are closest to commercial or industrial adoption?

The evidence suggests a hierarchy of adoption readiness:

- **Plasma treatment** appears closest to commercial use because it is already described as environmentally sustainable and as a way to replace hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. It is also being used to improve surface energy and adhesion properties [N3-R5].
- **Silane coupling agents** are well established and widely used, as they are explicitly described as common compatibilizers [N1-R4][N1-R5].
- **Alkali treatment** is highly cost-effective and attractive for industrial adoption, although it may still be limited by chemical residues or process constraints [N2-F2].
- **Bio-inspired coatings and nanoscale functionalization** are promising but still more research-oriented than fully industrialized, even though they are increasingly being evaluated for practical applications [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### 8) Sustainability and environmental implications

The environmental dimension is central. Natural fibers are promoted as eco-friendly, renewable, and biodegradable materials [N4-F4]. The broader environmental review notes that fiber-reinforced composites face significant environmental challenges throughout their lifecycle, including raw material extraction, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life [N6-R4]. At the same time, plasma treatment is positioned as environmentally sustainable and as a way to reduce hazardous chemical use [N1-F1]. This means that the best commercial path is not just to select the most effective treatment, but to choose the one that balances performance, cost, scalability, and environmental impact.

### 9) Summary table of the main techniques

If you want a quick summary, here is a concise table based on the evidence:

| Technique                | Type              | Functional groups/coating introduced | Primary compatibility mechanism            | Key benefit                         | Main limitation/trade-off                              |
|-------------------------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Silane coupling agents  | Chemical          | Silane-derived functional groups     | Interfacial bonding, wettability, adhesion | Strong compatibility, thermal stability | Can be less scalable or more expensive [N1-R4][N3-F3] |
| Plasma treatment        | Plasma-based      | Functionalization, grafting, polymerization | Wettability, adhesion, surface energy     | Environmentally sustainable, precise control [N1-F1] | High initial cost, operational constraints [N3-F3]     |
| Alkali treatment        | Chemical          | Roughened surface                   | Mechanical interlocking, cleaning          | Highly cost-effective [N2-F2]       | May leave chemical residues, limited by process constraints [N2-F2] |
| Other chemical treatments | Chemical         | Acetylation, benzoylation, steric acid treatment | Surface functionalization, wettability     | Broad compatibility, established use [N3-F3] | Can be expensive or operationally demanding [N2-F2]   |
| Physical methods        | Mechanical/physical | Surface roughening, dry cleaning      | Mechanical interlocking, surface energy    | Clean and environmentally friendly [N3-F3] | May have high initial costs [N3-F3]                    |

### 10) Bottom line

The most supported answer is:

**To enhance compatibility between natural fibers and polymer matrices in composites, the most commonly used fiber surface modification techniques are silane coupling agents, plasma treatment, and alkali treatment. Silane coupling agents are chemical and introduce silane-derived functional groups and coatings to improve wettability and interfacial adhesion [N1-R4][N1-F3]. Plasma treatment is plasma-based and improves surface energy, wettability, and adhesion through functionalization, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1][N3-R5]. Alkali treatment is chemical and cost-effective, creating a rough surface that supports mechanical interlocking and better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2]. These techniques are often combined or used sequentially, and emerging trends include bio-inspired coatings, nanoscale functionalization, and more sustainable surface engineering [N5-R1][N5-R3]. Plasma and silane remain the most established and industrially relevant methods, while newer approaches are increasingly promising for addressing existing limitations such as poor adhesion, moisture absorption, flammability, and environmental impact [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N6-R4].**

## Integrated summary of fiber surface modification techniques for natural fiber/polymer compatibility

Natural fiber composites are attractive because natural fibers are renewable, lightweight, and biodegradable, but they often have poor compatibility with polymer matrices due to differences in polarity, hydrophilicity, and surface chemistry. The literature shows that surface modification is the primary way to bridge this gap. The best-supported conclusion is that the major fiber surface modification techniques are **chemical, plasma-based, and mechanical/physical methods**, with **silane coupling agents**, **plasma treatment**, and **alkali treatment** being the most commonly used and most explicitly discussed in the evidence [N1-R4][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 1) Common modification techniques and their classification

The evidence identifies a clear inventory of major techniques:

- **Silane coupling agents**: These are explicitly described as compatibilizers between fibers and matrix that improve bond by removing weak boundary layers and creating a cross-linked region [N1-R4]. They are also among the most common chemical treatments, and silanization is noted as a widely used method to improve wettability and interfacial adhesion [N1-R5][N3-F3]. Silane treatment introduces **silane-derived functional groups** and a **thin protective coating**, which can improve wettability and interfacial bonding [N1-F3].

- **Plasma treatment**: This is described as an environmentally sustainable procedure for enhancing the surface characteristics of natural fibers [N1-R2]. The review explicitly states that low-temperature plasma surface treatment is used to tailor surface properties without affecting bulk properties [N1-F1]. Plasma processes include functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1]. Plasma treatment is especially associated with improving **hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy** [N1-F1][N3-R5].

- **Alkali treatment**: This is presented as a widely used and highly cost-effective treatment that removes non-cellulosic components and provides a clean but rough surface for better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2]. It is also part of the broader set of chemical treatments used to improve compatibility [N3-F3].

- **Other chemical and physical methods**: The evidence also mentions **mercierization, acetylation, benzoylation, steric acid treatment, and silanization** as chemical treatments, while physical methods are described as clean, dry, and free from expensive and environmentally unfriendly chemicals [N3-F3]. The interfacial adhesion review also notes that chemical modification can increase surface properties such as wettability, adhesion, surface tension, and fiber porosity [N2-R2].

- **Sequential or combined treatments**: The evidence repeatedly shows that treatments are often used **together** rather than in isolation. A clear example is the combination of **chemical and physical methods**, with silanization, plasma modification, and a combination of these methods being investigated [N3-F3]. Plasma research similarly suggests that multiple plasma processes can be used sequentially or in combination, including functionalization, ablation, ion implantation, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1].

### 2) How these techniques improve fiber-matrix compatibility

Surface treatments improve compatibility by altering **surface energy, wettability, and interfacial bonding**, and the evidence supports this with several overlapping mechanisms.

- **Wettability and surface energy**: Interdiffusion bonding is governed by wettability, and optimum surface energy and polarity on both fibers and matrix create permanent adhesion via Van der Waals, covalent, and electrostatic forces [N2-R1]. Chemical modification can also increase wettability, adhesion, surface tension, and fiber porosity [N2-R2]. Plasma treatment improves the surface energy of fibers, thereby improving their wettability and adhesion properties [N3-R5]. Plasma processing also alters natural fibers and sustainable polymeric derivatives for potential applications by changing hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy [N1-F1].

- **Interfacial bonding and mechanical performance**: The interfacial adhesion review states that appropriate physical or chemical treatments applied to the fibers can increase their compatibility with the polymer and enhance composite performance [N2-F2]. It also notes that fiber-matrix interfacial adhesion is among the most influential factors affecting the physical, mechanical, and thermal properties of plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites [N2-F2]. Silanization is reported to improve water resistance, increase surface wettability of natural fibers by polymers, and promote interfacial adhesion [N3-F3]. The review of natural fibers and composites similarly says that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the matrix and enhance composite performance [N4-F4].

- **Mechanical interlocking and roughness**: Alkali treatment creates a clean but rough surface, which increases the area available for mechanical interlocking and improves contact between fiber and matrix [N2-F2]. This roughness is part of why alkali-treated fibers are often used [N2-F2].

### 3) Evidence for improved interfacial bonding and mechanical performance

The evidence across the branch reports is consistent that treatments improve mechanical performance. For example:

- The plasma study reports that plasma treatment improves the wettability and adhesion properties of fibers, which is particularly relevant for compatibility with matrix systems [N3-R5].
- Silanization is reported to improve flammability, thermal stability, and wettability, contributing to the suitability of modified fibers for composites [N3-F3].
- The interfacial adhesion review explicitly states that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the polymer and enhance composite performance [N2-F2].
- The natural fiber composites review says that natural fiber composites combine good mechanical properties with low density and are used in various industries [N4-F4].

### 4) Known limitations and trade-offs

The evidence also makes clear that no single treatment is perfect. Each method has trade-offs:

- **Cost and scalability**: Alkali treatment is highly cost-effective [N2-F2], but other chemical treatments can be expensive and may require careful handling [N2-F2]. Physical methods are clean and dry but can have high initial system costs and operational constraints [N3-F3].
- **Environmental impact**: Plasma treatment is presented as environmentally sustainable and as a way to replace environmentally hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. However, the broader lifecycle of fiber-reinforced composites is still environmentally significant, with challenges from raw material extraction to end-of-life [N6-R4]. Natural fibers are eco-friendly and renewable, but they can still be limited by poor compatibility, moisture absorption, and flammability [N4-F4].
- **Functional specificity**: Silane coupling agents are effective and widely used, but they may be less scalable or more expensive than some physical methods [N1-R4][N3-F3]. Plasma treatment is effective and environmentally attractive, but its adoption depends on equipment costs and process constraints [N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests that the most effective strategy is often to combine chemical and physical treatments rather than rely on a single method [N3-F3].

### 5) Practical relevance and real-world application context

Treated natural fibers are already being used in a wide range of industries and composite systems:

- **Construction**: Natural fibers are described as reducing the carbon footprint of building materials and enhancing sustainability in construction [N6-R2].
- **Automotive**: Treated fibers are used in interior insulation, seat bottom, door panels, dashboard, body panels, boot liner, and other automotive components [N3-F3].
- **Aerospace, marine, and sporting goods**: The review says natural fiber composites are used in these sectors and are promoted as eco-friendly alternatives to conventional materials [N4-F4].
- **Packaging and structural applications**: Banana and sisal fiber-reinforced epoxy biocomposites were studied for structural applications [N4-F4], and hemp and banana fiber-fabric-reinforced polymer composites were studied for exterior-engineered parts [N4-R2].

The evidence also shows that treated natural fibers are used with a broad range of polymer matrices, including thermoplastics, thermosets, biodegradable polymers, bioplastics, and polymers derived from fossil resources [N4-F4]. This indicates that the compatibility improvements are not limited to a single matrix system.

### 6) Recent trends and emerging approaches

The evidence points to several recent trends that go beyond the traditional silane and plasma approaches:

- **Bio-inspired coatings**: One emerging approach is bio-inspired coatings for natural fiber composites, which the review says examines recent advancements in bio-inspired coatings and their unique properties [N5-R1].
- **Nanoscale functionalization**: The review of surface and interfacial engineering of biosourced fillers highlights recent developments in nanocellulose and 2D materials like graphene [N5-R3]. This suggests a shift toward more precise, nanoscale control of the fiber-matrix interface.
- **Silane-based surface modification**: Silane treatment is still central, but the evidence shows that it is increasingly understood in terms of mechanical, thermal, and interfacial properties [N5-R4].
- **Plasma surface engineering**: Plasma remains a major trend because it can functionalize, graft, polymerize, and otherwise alter surface chemistry in a controlled way [N1-F1].

These emerging approaches address existing limitations in several ways:

- They can improve precision and specificity of the surface chemistry introduced.
- They can reduce reliance on costly or toxic chemicals.
- They can address poor adhesion, moisture absorption, and flammability.
- They can support broader sustainability goals by using cleaner processes and bio-inspired designs.

### 7) Which approaches are closest to commercial or industrial adoption?

The evidence suggests a hierarchy of adoption readiness:

- **Plasma treatment** appears closest to commercial use because it is already described as environmentally sustainable and as a way to replace hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. It is also being used to improve surface energy and adhesion properties [N3-R5].
- **Silane coupling agents** are well established and widely used, as they are explicitly described as common compatibilizers [N1-R4][N1-R5].
- **Alkali treatment** is highly cost-effective and attractive for industrial adoption, although it may still be limited by chemical residues or process constraints [N2-F2].
- **Bio-inspired coatings and nanoscale functionalization** are promising but still more research-oriented than fully industrialized, even though they are increasingly being evaluated for practical applications [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### 8) Sustainability and environmental implications

The environmental dimension is central. Natural fibers are promoted as eco-friendly, renewable, and biodegradable materials [N4-F4]. The broader environmental review notes that fiber-reinforced composites face significant environmental challenges throughout their lifecycle, including raw material extraction, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life [N6-R4]. At the same time, plasma treatment is positioned as environmentally sustainable and as a way to reduce hazardous chemical use [N1-F1]. This means that the best commercial path is not just to select the most effective treatment, but to choose the one that balances performance, cost, scalability, and environmental impact.

### 9) Summary table of the main techniques

If you want a quick summary, here is a concise table based on the evidence:

|-------------------------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Silane coupling agents  | Chemical          | Silane-derived functional groups     | Interfacial bonding, wettability, adhesion | Strong compatibility, thermal stability | Can be less scalable or more expensive [N1-R4][N3-F3] |

### 10) Bottom line

The most supported answer is:

**To enhance compatibility between natural fibers and polymer matrices in composites, the most commonly used fiber surface modification techniques are silane coupling agents, plasma treatment, and alkali treatment. Silane coupling agents are chemical and introduce silane-derived functional groups and coatings to improve wettability and interfacial adhesion [N1-R4][N1-F3]. Plasma treatment is plasma-based and improves surface energy, wettability, and adhesion through functionalization, grafting, and polymerization [N1-F1][N3-R5]. Alkali treatment is chemical and cost-effective, creating a rough surface that supports mechanical interlocking and better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2]. These techniques are often combined or used sequentially, and emerging trends include bio-inspired coatings, nanoscale functionalization, and more sustainable surface engineering [N5-R1][N5-R3]. Plasma and silane remain the most established and industrially relevant methods, while newer approaches are increasingly promising for addressing existing limitations such as poor adhesion, moisture absorption, flammability, and environmental impact [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N6-R4].**

Surface treatments improve fiber-matrix compatibility by changing surface energy, wettability, and interfacial bonding. The evidence shows that interdiffusion bonding is governed by wettability, and optimum surface energy and polarity on both fibers and matrix create permanent adhesion via Van der Waals, covalent, and electrostatic forces [N2-R1]. The interfacial adhesion review also notes that chemical modification can increase surface properties such as wettability, adhesion, surface tension, and fiber porosity [N2-R2]. It further states that interfacial adhesion mechanisms include interdiffusion, electrostatic adhesion, chemical adhesion, and mechanical interlocking, and that a good interface condition is facilitated by one or a mixture of these mechanisms [N2-F2]. This indicates that the compatibility improvement is not only a direct surface effect, but also a multiscale interfacial phenomenon.

For plasma treatment, the evidence is especially strong on wettability and surface energy. Plasma treatment enhances the surface energy of fibers, improving wettability and adhesion properties [N3-R5]. The review of plasma research says that plasma processing alters the surface properties of natural fibers and sustainable polymeric derivatives, including hydrophilicity, adhesion, and surface energy [N1-F1]. This makes plasma one of the most direct ways to improve fiber-matrix compatibility through surface wetting. The same source also says that plasma can be used for functionalization, grafting, and polymerization, which suggests that it can introduce chemical functionality that further supports bonding [N1-F1].

Silane coupling agents are also strongly tied to improved wettability and interfacial adhesion. The review states that silanization can improve water resistance, increase surface wettability of natural fibers by polymers, and promote interfacial adhesion [N3-F3]. The same source notes that silane treatment is often used to improve the properties of natural fibers, including flammability, thermal stability, and wettability [N3-F3]. It also says that silane coupling agents are used as compatibilizers between fibers and matrix [N1-R4]. This means silane is not only a chemical treatment, but also a method of introducing specific functional groups that can bridge the fiber and matrix.

Alkali treatment improves compatibility through roughening and cleaning. The interfacial adhesion review describes alkali treatment as the most widely used treatment because it removes non-cellulosic components and offers a clean but rough surface for better interfacial adhesion [N2-F2]. This roughness increases the area available for mechanical interlocking and improves contact between fiber and matrix, which is part of why alkali-treated fibers are often used [N2-F2]. The review also says that chemical treatments such as mercerization, acetylation, benzoylation, steric acid treatment, and silanization are used to increase compatibility with matrix [N3-F3], and that silanization has a positive effect on interfacial adhesion [N3-F3]. This shows that alkali treatment can be complementary to other treatments rather than a standalone solution.

Evidence for improved interfacial bonding and mechanical performance comes from multiple sources. The interfacial adhesion review states that appropriate physical or chemical treatments applied to the fibers can increase their compatibility with the polymer, enhancing the performance of the composites [N2-F2]. It also notes that fiber-matrix interfacial adhesion is among the most influential factors affecting the physical, mechanical, and thermal properties of plant-fiber-reinforced polymer composites [N2-F2]. In the plasma study, the review says that plasma treatment improves the wettability and adhesion properties of fibers, which is particularly relevant for compatibility with matrix systems [N3-R5]. The silanization study reports that modified fibers show improved properties such as flammability reduction, thermal stability, and wettability, contributing to their suitability for composites [N3-F3]. The review of natural fibers and composites similarly says that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility with the matrix and enhance composite performance [N4-F4]. This pattern across sources supports the conclusion that treatments are effective when they improve both surface wettability and the underlying interfacial bond.

Known limitations or trade-offs are also evident. Plasma treatment is described as an environmentally sustainable procedure, but the evidence also notes that initial system costs can be high and operators may face operational constraints [N3-F3]. Alkali treatment is noted as highly cost-effective [N2-F2], but it is also a chemical treatment that can leave residual chemicals or require careful post-treatment handling. The same review emphasizes that natural fibers are used in composites reinforced with thermoplastics, thermosets, ceramic resins, biodegradable polymers, bioplastics, and polymers derived from fossil resources [N4-F4]. This indicates that treated natural fibers are not limited to a single matrix system but are integrated across a broad family of polymer matrices.

A specific example from the evidence is banana and sisal fiber-reinforced epoxy biocomposites, which were studied for structural applications [N4-F4]. The review also discusses hemp and banana fiber-fabric-reinforced polymer composites suitable for exterior-engineered parts [N4-R2]. These examples show that treated natural fibers are used in structural and exterior applications, not only as textiles but also in load-bearing or durable composite systems. The review further notes that natural fibers are used in interior insulation, seat bottom, door panels, dashboard, body panels, boot liner, and other automotive components [N3-F3], which underscores the automotive industry’s reliance on treated natural fibers for lightweight, biodegradable, and flammability-reduced parts.

Cost and scalability considerations are a major theme. Alkali treatment is described as highly cost-effective [N2-F2], which makes it attractive for industrial adoption. However, the same source notes that chemical treatments can be expensive and may require careful handling [N2-F2]. The plasma study says that physical methods are clean, dry, and free from expensive and environmentally unfriendly chemicals, but it also notes that initial system costs can be high and operators may face operational constraints [N3-F3]. This trade-off is important because scalability depends on whether the treatment can be applied efficiently at scale. The review of natural fibers and composites further says that the main limitation of natural fibers as reinforcement is the lack of compatibility between fibers and matrix, and that appropriate physical or chemical treatments can increase compatibility and enhance composite performance [N4-F4]. This implies that industrial adoption is constrained by both the need for effective treatment and the feasibility of applying it economically and at scale.

Environmental and sustainability implications are strong. The review says that natural fibers are eco-friendly, renewable, and biodegradable, and that natural fiber composites are promoted as sustainable materials that reduce environmental impact and support sustainable development [N4-F4]. The same review states that natural fibers reduce the carbon footprint of building materials and enhance the overall sustainability of construction [N6-R2]. Plasma treatment is presented as an environmentally sustainable procedure and as a way to reduce environmentally hazardous chemicals [N1-F1]. In practical terms, the evidence supports a picture of treated natural fibers being deployed in construction, automotive, aerospace, marine, and packaging industries, with composites including thermoplastics, thermosets, biodegradable polymers, and epoxy systems [N4-F4]. The environmental implication is that treated natural fibers are part of a sustainable materials strategy, but adoption depends on balancing mechanical performance, cost, and lifecycle environmental impact [N4-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].
